title: Evaluating transparency in AI/ML model characteristics for FDA-reviewed medical devices
paperTitle: Evaluating transparency in AI/ML model characteristics for FDA-reviewed medical devices
excerpt: Clear model and dataset documentation is essential for interpreting an AI device’s reported performance.
html:
What the paper explores

This study assessed transparency in publicly available FDA device summaries across model-development and performance-reporting categories. Using an AI Characteristics Transparency Reporting score, the authors found limited disclosure across many of the assessed characteristics, despite modest improvement after the period associated with good machine learning practice principles.

How to interpret the evidence

The score describes public reporting, not the complete regulatory submission or the inherent quality of every model. Missing public information should not be treated as proof that a study was not performed.

Questions for MedTech teams

Document model scope, data provenance, evaluation methods and limitations in a traceable form that connects technical work with clinical and regulatory communication.

title: Performance of Rapid Antigen Tests to Detect Symptomatic and Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 Infection : A Prospective Cohort Study
paperTitle: Performance of Rapid Antigen Tests to Detect Symptomatic and Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 Infection : A Prospective Cohort Study
excerpt: Why the timing and repetition of an antigen test matter as much as its single-test sensitivity.
html:
What the paper explores

This prospective US cohort paired home antigen testing with molecular testing every 48 hours. Performance differed by symptom status, and repeat testing improved detection. The study treats a sequence of tests as an evaluation strategy, rather than assuming one negative result answers the clinical question.

How to interpret the evidence

The tested interval was 48 hours. The results do not establish performance for shorter intervals, other products or every later viral variant.

Questions for MedTech teams

For an IVD study, define the intended population, testing schedule and interpretation of repeated results before selecting performance endpoints.

The evidence concerns a specific system, disease definition, operator training protocol and intended population. It does not validate other AI systems or justify broader clinical claims.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of covid-19 rapid antigen tests with unsupervised self-sampling in people with symptoms in the omicron period: cross sectional study
paperTitle: Diagnostic accuracy of covid-19 rapid antigen tests with unsupervised self-sampling in people with symptoms in the omicron period: cross sectional study
excerpt: Self-sampling, symptoms and the reason for testing can change the performance measured in a diagnostic study.
html:
What the paper explores

The investigators evaluated unsupervised rapid antigen self-tests among symptomatic people during the Omicron period in the Netherlands. Results varied with the sampling approach and with whether participants were already confirming a positive self-test. That recruitment context is an important part of interpreting the reported sensitivity.

How to interpret the evidence

This was a diagnostic accuracy study in a particular epidemic and recruitment setting. Its results should not be transferred directly to a different population. A published correction is linked below; consult the corrected article before using exact values.

Questions for MedTech teams

Document who enters the study, why they seek testing and how specimens are collected. Those details help explain what a reported performance estimate actually represents.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of rapid antigen tests in asymptomatic and presymptomatic close contacts of individuals with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection: cross sectional study
paperTitle: Diagnostic accuracy of rapid antigen tests in asymptomatic and presymptomatic close contacts of individuals with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection: cross sectional study
excerpt: A study of close contacts illustrates why intended-use populations and testing time must be defined together.
html:
What the paper explores

This cross-sectional study assessed rapid antigen testing in asymptomatic and presymptomatic close contacts of people with confirmed infection. Diagnostic sensitivity changed when the analysis considered subsequent symptoms or used a viral-load threshold as a proxy for infectiousness.

How to interpret the evidence

A viral-load threshold is a proxy, not a direct measurement of transmission. Findings from close contacts tested at a defined point after exposure do not establish accuracy for every screening use.

Questions for MedTech teams

Plan separate analyses for the intended clinical question. Detecting any infection and identifying a high viral-load subset are different evaluation targets.

excerpt: What a decentralized diagnostic study can teach us about enrollment, follow-up and paired sample collection.
html:
What the paper explores

The Test Us At Home study used digital recruitment and remote participation to evaluate repeated antigen testing. Participants completed antigen and molecular comparator testing on a defined schedule. The paper describes how a geographically distributed study could enroll participants during changing infection prevalence.

How to interpret the evidence

This is a study-design and implementation report. Operational feasibility does not by itself prove the performance of a new test, or guarantee that the same approach suits another population.

Questions for MedTech teams

Remote clinical operations still need clear instructions, sample logistics, traceable data and reliable follow-up. Treat these as parts of the evidence plan from the start.

title: Disparities in dermatology AI performance on a diverse, curated clinical image set
paperTitle: Disparities in dermatology AI performance on a diverse, curated clinical image set
excerpt: Diverse, clinically confirmed images reveal performance differences hidden by narrower evaluation datasets.
html:
What the paper explores

The Diverse Dermatology Images study assembled a curated, pathology-confirmed image dataset with varied skin tones and conditions. The authors found weaknesses in existing dermatology AI models, especially on darker skin tones and less common diseases. They also examined the effect of fine-tuning on representative data.

How to interpret the evidence

A curated dataset is an important evaluation tool, but it is not a substitute for prospective evidence in the intended clinical workflow. Findings depend on the models and image set examined.

Questions for MedTech teams

Plan representative data collection and subgroup evaluation before deployment. Aggregate accuracy can hide a product’s most consequential failure modes.

title: Detection and localization of surgically resectable cancers with a multi-analyte blood test
paperTitle: Detection and localization of surgically resectable cancers with a multi-analyte blood test
excerpt: Multi-analyte cancer detection shows why case-control performance and population screening are different questions.
html:
What the paper explores

CancerSEEK combined circulating protein measurements with cell-free DNA mutation analysis. The study evaluated patients with already diagnosed, nonmetastatic cancers and healthy controls, and explored whether positive results could narrow the likely anatomical origin of the cancer.

How to interpret the evidence

Performance in known cases and healthy controls cannot establish screening performance in an unselected population. Clinical benefit, downstream investigation and the consequences of false positives require separate evidence.

Questions for MedTech teams

For a new IVD, align the population and reference method with the proposed clinical use. The paper’s Johns Hopkins academic affiliations do not imply an affiliation with Hopkins MedTech.

title: Blood-based tests for multicancer early detection (PATHFINDER): a prospective cohort study
paperTitle: Blood-based tests for multicancer early detection (PATHFINDER): a prospective cohort study
excerpt: PATHFINDER examines what happens after a multicancer blood test returns a positive signal.
html:
What the paper explores

This prospective cohort evaluated the feasibility of a multicancer early detection blood test in adults without signs or symptoms of cancer. A positive signal initiated diagnostic assessment. The investigators measured the time and testing needed to reach a diagnostic resolution, including the experience of people with false-positive results.

How to interpret the evidence

A convenience cohort and feasibility outcomes do not establish a mortality benefit or settle the clinical utility of population screening. The cohort’s composition also matters when considering generalizability.

Questions for MedTech teams

Diagnostic evidence planning should include the pathway after the result: referrals, confirmatory procedures, time to resolution and potential harms.

html:
What the paper explores

This systematic review compared public 510(k) summaries with marketing materials for AI and machine-learning-enabled medical devices. The authors identified products whose public descriptions did not align clearly with their clearance documentation, illustrating the need to distinguish authorized intended use from promotional language.

How to interpret the evidence

The review covers a historical sample and publicly available documents. It is not a statement of current FDA policy, and absent details in a summary do not prove that FDA never reviewed them.

Questions for MedTech teams

Maintain traceability between the intended use, evidence, submission, labeling and website claims. Marketing review should be connected to regulatory document control.

The analysis reflects the information reported publicly. It cannot recover all discussions or data in a regulatory review, and it does not establish that a nonconcurrent design is unsuitable in every setting.

The findings concern historical panel-track supplements, rather than every type of device change or all supplement pathways. Study-design observations are not a device-specific regulatory determination.

What the paper explores

Wu and colleagues reviewed public FDA summaries for medical AI devices and conducted a case study of pneumothorax detection across hospital datasets. How to interpret the evidence

Public summaries do not contain every detail available during regulatory review. The work is a historical analysis, and the cross-site example concerns selected datasets and models.

Questions for MedTech teams

Specify independent evaluation settings, relevant subgroups and clinical workflow questions. Evidence of generalizability should go beyond a single performance number on one dataset.

The counts and technology observations describe the study’s historical dataset. They are not a live inventory of FDA authorizations or proof of the performance of any individual device.

paperTitle: Nationwide real-world implementation of AI for cancer detection in population-based mammography screening

html:
What the paper explores

PRAIM compared AI-supported double reading with standard double reading in organized mammography screening at multiple German sites. The study evaluated cancer detection and recall measures in actual clinical operations, extending the discussion beyond retrospective image classification.

How to interpret the evidence

Radiologists chose whether to use AI, so the observational design leaves room for selection and confounding. Improved screening metrics do not by themselves establish a reduction in mortality.

Questions for MedTech teams

Real-world evaluation should account for deployment choices, site variation and the clinical pathway, with outcomes selected for the intended use.

title: A Cell-free DNA Blood-Based Test for Colorectal Cancer Screening
paperTitle: A Cell-free DNA Blood-Based Test for Colorectal Cancer Screening
excerpt: Blood-based colorectal cancer screening makes the distinction between cancer and precancer endpoints especially clear.
html:
What the paper explores

The ECLIPSE study evaluated a cell-free DNA blood test in a screening-eligible population against colonoscopy. The reported performance differed substantially for colorectal cancer and advanced precancerous lesions, showing why these outcomes should be presented separately rather than combined into a single claim.

How to interpret the evidence

Diagnostic accuracy alone does not establish improved screening adherence or reduced mortality. The study’s findings apply to the assessed assay and population.

Questions for MedTech teams

Define clinically meaningful endpoints in advance. A test’s ability to identify existing cancer and its ability to detect precursors answer different screening questions.

What the paper explores

The BLUE-C study evaluated a next-generation multitarget stool DNA test in asymptomatic adults undergoing screening colonoscopy. It compared performance with a fecal immunochemical test. How to interpret the evidence

A diagnostic accuracy comparison does not establish every downstream clinical benefit or the best strategy for each person. The tradeoff must be interpreted within the intended screening pathway.

Questions for MedTech teams

Plan comparative endpoints and how false positives and false negatives will be interpreted. A useful performance claim should present both detection and exclusion of disease.

What the paper explores

The TRIPOD+AI statement updates reporting recommendations for studies that develop or evaluate clinical prediction models. It brings regression and machine-learning approaches into a common framework intended to improve completeness, accuracy and transparency of reporting.

Questions for MedTech teams

Maintain clear records of model development and evaluation so that readers can distinguish the question studied, the data used and the evidence needed before implementation.

excerpt: CLAIM provides a structured way to report AI research in medical imaging.
html:
What the paper explores

This journal editorial introduces the Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging. It adapts established reporting principles to applications including classification, image reconstruction, text analysis and workflow optimization, emphasizing sufficient methodological detail for critical review and reproducibility.

How to interpret the evidence

CLAIM is a reporting framework rather than a clinical validation study or regulatory standard. A complete manuscript can still describe a model with limited generalizability.

Questions for MedTech teams

Use a clear reporting structure to connect data selection, methods and results. Review subsequent versions of reporting frameworks before applying them to a new study.
